item.title: NCAA created this mess, now LSU set to make Dae’Quan Wright college football’s first NFL returnee
item.description: A Louisiana court is shielding LSU from NCAA punishment as Lane Kiffin prepares to welcome Dae'Quan Wright in a unprecedented NFL-to-college transfer.
item.content:encoded:
Former Ole Miss tight end Dae’Quan Wright could make history this week by becoming the first player to jump from the NFL back to college football — with LSU coach Lane Kiffin at the center of this new development.

In what has become one of the wildest offseasons in recent memory, college athletics is reeling from a wave of lawsuits filed against the NCAA by athletes in the 2022 recruiting class.

After filing suit in a Louisiana court last week, plaintiffs received a temporary restraining order from 19th Judicial District Court Judge Will Jorden in Baton Rouge.

NFL TO NCAA? COURTROOM CHAOS IS GIVING PRO ATHLETES A BIZARRE PATH BACK TO COLLEGE, AND IT'S ONLY JUST BEGUN

The ruling opened a makeshift transfer portal that was viable for only one week, allowing a number of athletes to contemplate an unprecedented move: participating in NFL training camp one week, then enrolling in college classes the next.

On Sunday night, Cleveland Browns head coach Todd Monken was left flabbergasted by the situation. It involved a call from Kiffin last week that he did not return.

What was the call about? Monken implied following the Browns’ preseason game that it centered on Wright, who dressed Saturday night but did not play.

"Man, isn't this s--- crazy?" Todd Monken told reporters. "I don't even know what to say. ... I wondered why Lane Kiffin reached out to me a week ago, now I know. I didn't call him back; I guess I should have."

While the Tenth Circuit in Colorado granted a stay last week in the Wisne v. NCAA case — halting the blanket waiver that had allowed members of the 2022 class to join any team willing to take them — the decision only opened the door for more lawsuits at the state level.

NCAA WINS TENTH CIRCUIT 'STAY', BUT FACES MORE ELIGIBILITY LAWSUITS FROM 2022 CLASS ATHLETES IN CHAOTIC TIME

One of those cases was filed just a few miles from LSU’s campus. And Kiffin appears more than willing to welcome one of his former Ole Miss players back to college for another season.

If you were unaware, the conference has a rule in place that prohibits athletes from transferring to another SEC school outside of the normal portal period.

The rule, which dates back to former Alabama defensive back Mo Smith, makes it a point to emphasize that an athlete cannot make a move like Dae'Quan Wright is trying to pull off.

Under normal circumstances, Wright would not be allowed to play for Ole Miss in 2025 and then LSU in 2026 if the transfer is made outside of the NCAA's transfer portal period.

But technically, there is no rule pertaining to a player going from an SEC school to the NFL, and then back to another conference program within the same year.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

And, according to the court order granted by Judge Will Jorden of Louisiana, any school that takes an athlete protected by the previously mentioned temporary order cannot be punished by the NCAA or conference for adding a player like Dae'Quan Wright to the roster.

This could also lead to former LSU edge rusher Jack Pyburn making a return to Baton Rouge this week as well.

TENNESSEE COACH UNLOADS ON NCAA'S 'BULLS–T', AFTER STAR LINEBACKER SUSPENDED FOR OUTDATED RULE

Remember Tennessee linebacker Arion Carter?

He's preparing to serve a two-game suspension for accepting a $427 plane ticket after declaring for the NFL after the 2025 season.

Just a few weeks later, after finding out he had a foot injury that would prevent him from preparing for the draft, he took himself out of the process and returned to Tennessee. Because he hired an agent and took a small amount of money, the NCAA suspended him for two-games.

Now? I wouldn’t blame Carter if he chose the sue the NCAA in hopes of being granted a ruling that would allow him to play immediately.

What is being forgotten by some during this whole kerfuffle is that it essentially comes down to the school president.

If LSU's Wade Rousse wanted to avoid having his school in this ongoing mess, he could easily tell Lane Kiffin to just back down.

The same could be said for athletic director Verge Ausberry. But, why would one school say 'no' to something that opponents could easily take advantage of as well?

So, it's hard to blame the school for the NCAA's doing, even if that sounds like an excuse.

NCAA IGNORED THE WARNINGS. NOW IT'S FIGHTING FOR SURVIVAL IN COURTROOMS ACROSS AMERICA OVER ELIGIBILITY

The same folks who are complaining about the current mess in college athletics are the same ones who are inviting the chaos through their front door.

Again though, it's pretty hard to put this on the schools, especially when the door has been opened.

But please, save us from the talking points around the 'Protect College Sports Act' that is currently floundering around the Senate.

"I think there’s a lot of negatives that are involved around this," Oregon's Dan Lanning told the media following Oregon's practice on Saturday. "One, once you go to the NFL, to me, you’re in the NFL. You don’t get the opportunity to come back. Two, most of us have built our rosters and you have a limited roster limit now.

"So if you invited somebody back to your team, that means you’re kicking somebody else off your team to match your roster limits. I don’t think that’s fair to the players that worked all summer, all spring and put themselves in position to be ready to work for a team to have somebody come back."

As for what's next with Dae'Quan Wright and LSU, it will obviously be an entertaining week in Baton Rouge.

Who's next?

item.title: Shelley Fabares, star of 'The Donna Reed Show' and 'Coach,' dead at 82
item.description: Shelley Fabares starred on "The Donna Reed Show," hit No. 1 with "Johnny Angel" and earned two Emmy nods for "Coach" over a career spanning decades.
item.content:encoded:
Shelley Fabares, the actress and singer who starred in "The Donna Reed Show" and earned two Emmy nominations for her role in "Coach," has died. She was 82.

Fabares died Saturday in Los Angeles surrounded by her loved ones, her family confirmed in a statement to the Associated Press. Her cause of death was not disclosed.

"To her family and friends, Shelley was a source of love, strength, laughter, and comfort," her family wrote, according to the outlet. "She had a remarkable ability to make people feel welcomed, valued, and cared for."

'GOMER PYLE: USMC' STAR RONNIE SCHELL DEAD AT 94 AFTER DECADES-LONG CAREER

"We will remember Shelley for her kindness, loyalty, wit, courage, and beautiful spirit. We will miss her deeply — not only as a celebrated performer, but as the loving and extraordinary person she was in our everyday lives," they added.

Fabares became one of television's most recognizable young stars when she was cast as Mary Stone, the teenage daughter of the characters played by Donna Reed and Carl Betz, on "The Donna Reed Show" in 1958.

During her time on the hit family sitcom, Fabares unexpectedly launched a successful recording career after the show's producer, Tony Owen, decided to incorporate singing into the series.

The actress' debut single, "Johnny Angel," reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1962 and sold more than 1 million copies. She released several albums and scored additional hits with "Johnny Loves Me" and "The Things We Did Last Summer," though she later acknowledged that she never considered herself much of a singer.

Fabares left "The Donna Reed Show" as a regular cast member in 1963 but returned for guest appearances before the series ended in 1966. She remained close to Reed, whom she credited as a mentor who helped her navigate Hollywood as a young actress.

At the height of her teen idol fame, Fabares transitioned to the big screen and starred opposite Elvis Presley in three movies: "Girl Happy" in 1965, "Spinout" in 1966 and "Clambake" in 1967.

She also appeared in the 1964 surf movie "Ride the Wild Surf," the 1966 musical comedy "Hold On!" with Herman’s Hermits and the 1968 Hank Williams Jr. film "A Time to Sing."

Born Michele Ann Marie Fabares on Jan. 19, 1944, in Santa Monica, California, she was the niece of actress Nanette Fabray. Fabares began modeling as a young child and made her television debut at age 10 on an episode of "Letter to Loretta."

Her early credits included appearances in "The Bad Seed," "Never Say Goodbye," "Jeanne Eagels" and "Marjorie Morningstar." She also appeared with Annette Funicello in the 1958 Disney serial "Annette."

After her initial success as a teen star, Fabares built a prolific television career that spanned several decades. In 1971, she portrayed Joy Piccolo, the wife of Chicago Bears running back Brian Piccolo, whom James Caan played, in the acclaimed television movie "Brian's Song," which also starred Billy Dee Williams.

Fabares later held regular roles on "The Brian Keith Show," "The Practice" and "Forever Fernwood." From 1978 to 1984, she played Francine Webster, the professional rival of Bonnie Franklin’s Ann Romano, on "One Day at a Time."

She also made guest appearances on television shows, including "The Twilight Zone," "Mannix," "The Rockford Files," "The Love Boat," "Fantasy Island," "Mork & Mindy" and "Murder, She Wrote."

item.title: The Athletic probes Dianna Russini and Mike Vrabel relationship while considering getting in bed with the NFL
item.description: The Athletic is in talks to place content on NFL.com while simultaneously investigating Dianna Russini's possible conflict of interest with Mike Vrabel.
item.content:encoded:
The line between the NFL and the journalists that cover the league has gotten somewhat blurred recently and the latest example of that trend is The Athletic engaging in discussions with the NFL to add its content on the league's signature website.

As Front Office Sports reported recently, and a source confirmed to OutKick on Sunday, the New York Times-owned sports vertical and the NFL have held discussions about expanding their relationship.

And while the primary subject of those talks is said to be about video content, the idea of possibly including written content from the The Athletic on NFL.com and the NFL+ app has been part of discussions, the source confirmed.

THE ATHLETIC EXECUTIVE EDITOR ADMITS KEY MISTAKE MADE IN HANDLING OF DIANNA RUSSINI CONTROVERSY: REPORT

It is unclear how far along these talks about collaboration are but what is certain is that if they reach an agreement to indeed place The Athletic stories on the NFL media website, multiple thorny issues will be raised.

Let's begin here:

The Athletic is currently believed to be conducting an internal probe on the work of its former NFL reporter Dianna Russini as it pertains to a possible conflict of interest she may have had with New England Patriots coach Mike Vrabel.

So, The Athletic is presumably in the throes of this conflict of interest investigation of a former reporter with an NFL coach while at the same time engaging in talks to enter into a conflict of interest situation with the NFL.

Got it.

People who kept abreast of the Russini-Vrabel news can understand the relationship extended beyond professional. That was amplified by the Page Six photos of Russini and Vrabel hugging, holding hands, and lounging by a pool and a hot tub at a Sedona, Arizona resort last spring.

DIANNA RUSSINI RESIGNS FROM THE ATHLETIC AMID MIKE VRABEL CONTROVERSY

The photos suggested something more intimate than a typically accepted reporter-coach relationship and Vrabel admitted he eventually had to have difficult conversations with his family, including his wife, and even sought family counseling to address the situation.

That raises a sizeable inconsistency. The Athletic is presumably investigating Russini for possibly engaging in a questionable relationship with an NFL coach at a time it is weighing whether to get in bed with the NFL.

The Athletic's journalists are schooled on the vertical's editorial guidelines, most of them derived from The Times.

"When reporting and writing stories we do not have an agenda and it is important that our readers understand that," the section on transparency reads. "If our readers question our adherence to that basic tenet of journalism, our credibility will be at stake.

"To maintain the highest form of authority we should avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest and reveal ... sources or affiliations that may put into question our ability to be credible."

NFL PUTS 'INSPIRE CHANGE' AND 'CHOOSE LOVE' ON FIELDS BUT NOT SO AGGRESSIVE ABOUT ITS DOMESTIC ABUSE ISSUES

So will The Athletic, on the one hand trying to avoid the appearance of a conflict of interest, allow an affiliation with the NFL that violates its own guidelines by calling into question its credibility?

And such a move would indeed put into question The Athletic's ability to be credible if the content shared on the NFL site declines to address unflattering or controversial issues of domestic violence, suspensions, poor officiating, or the NFL's political agenda – which can be both left- and right-leaning at times.

Finally, The Athletic has over the last decade been a subscription-based service. The NFL's news website is not.

That's not a journalistic conflict of interest issue. But if The Athletic gives over its content to the NFL for free reader consumption, it does become a financial conflict of interest question within the company that readers will ultimately judge.

item.title: Fever coach dismisses Enes Kanter Freedom’s women’s sports fight as a 'social media thing'
item.description: Natasha Cloud shouted at Enes Kanter Freedom during a third-quarter timeout before security ejected him from Wintrust Arena in the Fever's win.
item.content:encoded:
Indiana Fever head coach Stephanie White urged reporters not to give Sunday’s courtside confrontation at Wintrust Arena any more attention, calling it a "social media thing," after Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected following a verbal clash with Chicago Sky guard Natasha Cloud.

Freedom has spent weeks exposing the WNBA’s cowardice on transgender eligibility, demanding the league protect biological women from male competition.

The Fever coach made clear she would rather bury the discussion than confront it.

"I mean, I think it's important that people like you guys in this room don't give it any gas, right? Like it's a social media thing," White told reporters when asked about the incident postgame.

During a third-quarter timeout with Indiana leading 81-75, Cloud began shouting toward Freedom at courtside and Freedom responded, prompting security to escort the former NBA center from the arena as the Fever went on to pull away for a 113-90 win.

Tensions were already high before the ejection.

Before tipoff, Freedom was shouted at and flipped off by fans, and security had to guide him through a hostile crowd outside Wintrust Arena.

Freedom later talked to OutKick and spoke about what went down. He said he believed his shirt, which contained the definition of a woman, was what triggered Cloud.

"I was cheering for my friend Sophie because when she shot that three, I put my hands in the air," Freedom said. "A couple possessions later, she came back and said, ‘She’s not gonna sleep with you.’ And I was shocked. I was like, ‘Listen, I’m not trying to sleep with her. I think she’s awesome. She’s a good friend.’ But I think it has a lot to do with my shirt.

"I was obviously wearing a shirt explaining what a woman is, and I think that had a lot to do with what she thinks about women. I think it triggered her a lot."

And it's not just a Chicago problem.

Last month in Seattle, Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton confronted two teenage fans holding signs in support of Fever guard Sophie Cunningham and reportedly called them "f—ing insane."

The WNBA suspended Keaton from five home games and fined her over the incident.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS SPORTS

Freedom’s ejection was the latest moment White is trying to wave away as "social media," even though the WNBA firestorm began when Cunningham said biological men do not belong in women’s sports and that young girls deserve protection.

At an Indiana Fever-Atlanta Dream game earlier this month, WNBA security told a mother and her teenage daughter to cover their pro-women’s-sports shirts or get tossed. The league later admitted it never should have happened.

Freedom then declared for the 2027 WNBA Draft, while former NBA player Royce White announced a similar bid. WNBA leadership has held meetings to address the issue but has not provided a clear public answer on transgender eligibility.

When Sky players Azura Stevens and Aicha Coulibaly were asked about Freedom’s ejection, Stevens said security had handled it.

"There was just a fan incident and the security handled it," Stevens said. "We’re going to just focus on the game."

Sky coach Tyler Marsh also backed Cloud, saying, "We all embrace her as someone who protects our team and protects people who need to be protected."

Meanwhile, Fever superstar Caitlin Clark said she did not see the confrontation.

Fever players said they had no interaction with Freedom during the game.

"To be honest, I didn't see it," Clark said. "We were talking about it the next play in our huddle, so I think that's probably a question for Chicago."

White can tell reporters to stop "giving it any gas," but the WNBA cannot dismiss this as social media when the dispute keeps producing confrontations, ejections and suspensions.

item.title: Ancient clue cracks open a 2,000-year-old mystery near famed Colosseum
item.description: Archaeologists working near Rome's Colosseum uncovered eight rooms with mosaics and painted decorations that may belong to an ancient Roman firehouse.
item.content:encoded:
Archaeologists digging near Rome's Colosseum believe they may have found an ancient firehouse dating back nearly 2,000 years.

The building, which dates to the second century A.D., was found in the Villa Celimontana park near the Colosseum, Reuters reported this month.

Villa Celimontana dates to the 16th century, when it was developed as a noble residence on Caelian Hill, one of the seven hills of ancient Rome.

CONSTRUCTION WORKERS CLEARING OLD BOMBS UNEXPECTEDLY FIND 'IMPORTANT' ANCIENT SANCTUARY

The discovery was originally announced by Rome's archaeological superintendency, part of Italy's Ministry of Culture.

At the excavation site, archaeologists fully uncovered five of the building's eight rooms, which contain mosaics and remnants of painted decorations.

Officials believe the building may have been part of the nearby barracks of the Fifth Cohort of the Vigiles, ancient Rome's firefighting force.

They cited one telling clue: A mosaic found at the site closely resembles one previously discovered in a firefighters' barracks in Ostia, ancient Rome's port city.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER SPRAWLING ROMAN ESTATE BURIED FOR CENTURIES BENEATH FARMLAND

The Vigiles were also tasked with maintaining public order at night, and their nearby barracks used water from an aqueduct.

"If this hypothesis is confirmed, the discovery would help reassess the extent of one of the most important military complexes of imperial Rome," officials said in a statement.

Pictures show the remains of the ancient building, including exposed walls and sections uncovered during the excavation.

Other images show fragments of mosaic uncovered at the site.

"Only a thorough study of the excavation materials and the structures exposed will provide further information on the newly discovered structure," the superintendency said.
